hook.text: A classifier answers in one pass through its model. A language model writes its answer one token at a time, and every token is another pass.

hook-cost.text: That's why generation is slow, and why it's hungry for memory. Four questions, all on one model: seventy billion parameters, served from eight GPUs.

q1.text: Question one. Why is LLM inference split into prefill and decode? Because generating a response has two phases, with different bottlenecks.

q1-prefill.text: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass. That's large matrix multiplication, so it's compute-bound, and it sets the time to first token, or TTFT.

q1-decode.text: Decode then produces one token per step. Each step reads every weight and the whole cached context to do a little arithmetic, so it's bound by memory bandwidth, and it sets the time per output token.

q1-reuse.text: Count it. With a two-thousand-token prompt, prefill puts every weight it reads to work two thousand times. A decode step for one request uses it once.

q1-levers.text: So the levers differ. A chat product cares most about TTFT and smooth streaming; an offline summarization job, about throughput and cost per request. Long prompts make prefill expensive, and long answers make decode expensive.

q1-follow.text: The follow-up: users wait seconds before any text appears, and then it streams quickly. That's prefill. Shorten the prompt, or cache a long shared prefix. Waiting to fill a bigger batch first would only add delay.

q2-in.text: Every decode step also reads the cached context, and that cache is the part that grows.

q2.text: Question two. What is the KV cache, and how large does it get? During decode, each new token attends to every token before it. Recomputing their keys and values at every step would be quadratic waste, so they're cached.

q2-formula.text: Per sequence, its size is two, for one key and one value, times the layers, the KV heads, the head dimension, the tokens, and the bytes per value.

q2-model.text: This model has eighty layers and eight KV heads of dimension a hundred and twenty-eight, at sixteen bits. That's three hundred and twenty kibibytes for every token.

q2-context.text: One context of a hundred and twenty-eight K tokens takes forty gibibytes, beside about a hundred and forty gigabytes of weights.

q2-fit.text: Now the last step, the one to do on the whiteboard: how many requests fit? Eight eighty-gigabyte GPUs, minus the weights, leave five hundred gigabytes. At eight K tokens a request, at most a hundred and eighty-six fit.

q2-long.text: At a hundred and twenty-eight K, eleven. Memory, not compute, usually caps how many requests a GPU serves at once, and this cache is where the memory goes.

q2-gqa.text: That's why grouped-query attention matters: several query heads share one key and value head. Give each of the sixty-four query heads its own, and the cache grows eight times: twenty-three of those eight K requests, not a hundred and eighty-six.

q3-in.text: So memory caps the batch, and the next question is how to keep it full.

q3.text: Question three. What are continuous batching and PagedAttention? Batching lets one read of the weights serve many sequences at once. The catch is that answers end at different lengths.

q3-static.text: Static batching groups requests and waits until the longest one finishes, so the slots that finished early sit idle.

q3-cont.text: Continuous batching, also called in-flight batching, admits a new request at any decode step, and releases a finished one immediately.

q3-sim.text: In a simulation, eight slots work through a thousand requests whose answers run from ten to a thousand tokens, most of them short. Static batching keeps the slots busy thirty-seven percent of the time. Continuous batching, ninety-nine.

q3-mem.text: Every busy slot needs cache memory, and no one knows in advance how long an answer will be. Reserve eight K tokens for a request that ends up using two thousand, and three quarters of its buffer sits empty.

q3-paged.text: PagedAttention stores the cache in fixed-size blocks, the way an operating system pages memory, and hands out blocks as the answer grows. With blocks of sixteen tokens, the only waste is the unfilled end of a request's last block: under one percent of two thousand. And requests that share a prompt prefix can share its blocks.

q3-paper.text: Less waste means more requests in the batch. PagedAttention came with vLLM, an open-source serving engine, whose paper reported two to four times the throughput of earlier systems at the same latency.

q3-latency.text: Notice that last part. A bigger batch raises throughput while each user's tokens arrive more slowly, so a throughput number only means something at a stated latency.

q4-in.text: The last two levers make every byte read go further.

q4.text: Question four. What do quantization and speculative decoding trade? Quantization stores the weights, and sometimes the KV cache, in fewer bits: eight or four instead of sixteen.

q4-bytes.text: Decode is bound by bandwidth, so moving fewer bytes makes it faster as well as smaller. At four bits, this model's weights shrink from about a hundred and forty gigabytes to thirty-five, a quarter of the weight bytes every step reads.

q4-fit.text: They'd fit on one of those GPUs, with room left for sixteen eight K requests.

q4-risk.text: The price is quality. It often slips on reasoning and rare cases before it shows in average perplexity, and your hardware may lack fast kernels for the format. So evaluate on your own task, not a generic benchmark.

q4-spec.text: Speculative decoding lets a small draft model propose several tokens, and the large model verify them all in one forward pass, which costs about one decode step, since reading the weights dominates either way. With the standard acceptance rule, the output distribution doesn't change, so quality isn't the price.

q4-sim.text: The speedup depends on how often the draft is right. In a simulation with four-token drafts, if each drafted token is accepted nine times in ten, a pass of the large model yields about four tokens. At half, under two.

q4-cost.text: And the draft model costs time and memory of its own, so it helps most on predictable text, and can lose where the draft is usually wrong.

rapid-in.text: Five more levers, one line each.

r-prefix.text: Prefix caching: compute a shared system prompt's cache once, so each request's prefill covers only what comes after it.

r-route.text: Routing: send the easy requests to a smaller model.

r-distill.text: Distillation: train a small model to imitate the large one on a narrow task.

r-stream.text: And streaming, which cuts the wait you feel rather than the work: the reader starts while the rest is still being written.

close.text: Most of these come down to bytes: the weights each step reads, and the cache each request holds.

next.text: But fast and cheap isn't enough if you can't tell whether the answers are good. Next: evaluating LLM systems.

r-reason.text: Reasoning budget: a model's thinking tokens are decode steps the user waits through before the first visible word, so spend them only on requests that need them.
